Over time, unstable pressure damages

thinking centers. This damage happens

pattern most people miss. The key blood
pressure pattern that predicts memory
loss years before it shows up is
something called pulse pressure. Pulse
pressure is simply the difference
between the top and bottom numbers on a
basic blood pressure reading. So, for
example, if you have a blood pressure of
150 over 70, the pulse pressure would be
150 minus 70 or 80. That gap is the
danger. A wide pulse pressure means the
top number is high and the bottom number
is low. And this usually happens as we
age. Why? Because arteries become stiff.
Instead of gently expanding with each
heartbeat, they snap back hard, sending
pressure waves straight to the brain.
Those pressure waves stress tiny brain
vessels, cause microscopic brain
injuries, reduce oxygen delivery, and
speed up brain aging. Over time, this
leads to white matter damage, slower
thinking, memory gaps, and a higher
dementia risk. Studies show that people
with wide pulse pressure have a
significantly increased risk of
cognitive decline, even if their normal
blood pressure readings are considered
to be okay. Here's why pulse pressure
tends to fly under the radar. Most blood
pressure checks happen once in a rushed
setting and usually while you're
stressed. Doctors often focus on is the
top number under control and is the

sleep on your side. And if you snore
